newsitem.title: USA: Arafat and Netanyahu could meet soon over Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Arafat and Netanyahu could meet soon over Hebron.

text.p: Efforts are under way to fix a meeting this weekend in Cairo between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to try to clinch a deal on the West Bank town of Hebron, Arab officials said on Thursday.

"The talk is that this meeting could be held tomorrow or the day after, but this is not certain," Osama El-Baz, chief foreign policy adviser to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, told reporters at a Washington seminar on the Middle East.
However, Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, general secretary of the Palestinian Authority cabinet, said the possible dates were Friday or Sunday, because Saturday is the Jewish sabbath.
Abdel-Rahman said he understood the meeting, if it went ahead, would be held in the Egyptian capital under the personal auspices of Mubarak.

Dennis Ross, U.S. special Middle East coordinator, said no firm arrangements had yet been met. "The important thing is that they are talking about having a meeting. At this point, a meeting has not been set up," he told journalists.

Earlier on Thursday, Arafat said in Gaza he was prepared to meet Netanyahu to discuss a long-delayed Hebron accord providing for Israeli forces to withdraw from most of the West Bank city. Netanyahu had called on Wednesday for such a meeting.

For two months Israel and the PLO have been negotiating details of a deal signed by Israel's previous government under which the Jewish state is to hand 80 percent of the city over to Palestinian rule. Each side blames the other for the delay.

Baz said the meeting between Arafat and Netanyahu, who last met in Washington two months ago, had not yet been fixed definitively because of remaining problems with the agreement on Hebron, where 400 Jews live among 100,000 Arabs.

He said these related to Israeli right of hot pursuit into PLO-controlled areas of the town, the arming of Palestinian police, and the reopening of Hebron's Shohada (Martyrs) Street linking Jewish and Arab areas.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said at the State Department the two sides were "nearing a conclusion" on Hebron. "The parties are edging closer together... but there are tough issues that remain to be worked out," he said.

Earlier, former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker called on the Clinton administration to take a stronger role to boost the flagging Middle East peace process and accused it of failing to speak out on Jewish settlements.

"Now that the presidential election in the United States is over it is essential, I think, that the United States assume a stronger leadership role to get the peace process back on track," Baker told the seminar.

He said this was "an important question" for the second administration of Democratic President Bill Clinton, re-elected to a new four-year term last month. Clinton on Thursday named U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright as secretary of state to replace Christopher, who retires next month.

Baker, who helped convene the landmark Madrid Middle East peace conference in 1991 under Republican President George Bush, said Washington had to tell "upsetting truths," a task he said had not come naturally to the present administration.
Baker said he was shocked by Christopher's decision to tone down U.S. criticism of Jewish settlements in the occupied territories, which Netanyahu has vowed to expand.
"Where are the United States voices today in opposition to increased settlement activity?" he asked.

Ross, in a address to the seminar, promised only a "continuing American commitment" to the Middle East in the next administration. "I would not expect to see any dramatic changes" under Albright, he said in response to a question.
"What we will not do is take the place of the parties," he said. "We can help but we can't do it for them."
